investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why does ¹⁸F-FDG accumulate in malignant cells?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: FDG is a glucose analogue taken up via GLUT transporters (upregulated in cancer) and phosphorylated by hexokinase to FDG-6-phosphate, which cannot be metabolised further or dephosphorylated, so it becomes metabolically trapped in proportion to glycolytic rate.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the SUV and what is it used for?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The standardised uptake value is a semi-quantitative measure of tracer activity normalised to injected dose and body weight. SUVmax helps characterise lesions and assess treatment response but is not diagnostic on its own.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the key patient-preparation steps before FDG PET-CT.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Fast for at least 6 hours
  • control blood glucose (ideally <11 mmol/L)
  • rest quietly and stay warm during the ~60 min uptake period
  • and avoid strenuous exercise for 24 h beforehand

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name common sites of physiological FDG uptake that can mimic pathology.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Brain
  • myocardium
  • renal collecting system/ureters/bladder (excretion)
  • bowel
  • brown fat (neck/supraclavicular/paravertebral) and skeletal muscle

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which tumours characteristically show low or absent FDG uptake (false negatives)?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Low-grade/indolent tumours
  • mucinous and lepidic adenocarcinomas
  • well-differentiated HCC
  • prostate cancer and renal cell carcinoma
  • also lesions below scanner resolution (sub-centimetre)

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is dietary preparation essential before cardiac FDG-PET?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Normal myocardium avidly takes up glucose (and therefore FDG), masking pathology. A prolonged high-fat, low/zero-carbohydrate diet followed by a fast (± IV heparin) switches myocytes to free-fatty-acid metabolism, suppressing physiological uptake so inflammatory/infective foci become visible.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What FDG pattern suggests active cardiac sarcoidosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Focal or focal-on-diffuse patchy FDG uptake not respecting coronary territories. Combined with a rest perfusion study, a perfusion–metabolism mismatch (reduced perfusion + increased FDG) indicates active, potentially reversible inflammation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does FDG-PET feature in the diagnosis of prosthetic-valve endocarditis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Abnormal FDG uptake around the prosthetic valve is a major criterion in the ESC-modified Duke criteria for prosthetic-valve endocarditis. FDG-PET/CT also detects lead, generator-pocket, vascular-graft and metastatic septic foci.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the main cause of a non-diagnostic cardiac FDG-PET, and the chief false positive?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Inadequate dietary suppression leaving residual physiological myocardial uptake is the commonest cause of a non-diagnostic study. Recent cardiac surgery or device implantation causes post-operative inflammatory FDG uptake, a key false positive.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the mechanism and approximate radiation dose of FDG-PET/CT?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: 18F-FDG is a glucose analogue taken up by GLUT transporters, phosphorylated and trapped in metabolically active cells. A typical FDG-PET/CT delivers roughly 6–10 mSv (tracer plus CT); standard pregnancy/breastfeeding precautions apply.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is PSMA and why is it a good imaging target in prostate cancer?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Prostate-specific membrane antigen is a transmembrane glycoprotein (glutamate carboxypeptidase II) overexpressed on prostate cancer cells, with expression rising with higher grade and stage. Radiolabelled ligands bind and are internalised, giving high tumour-to-background contrast.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name the two common PSMA PET radiotracers and a key difference.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁶⁸Ga-PSMA-11 (gallium-68, half-life ~68 min, generator-produced, imaged locally) and ¹⁸F-DCFPyL (fluorine-18, half-life ~110 min, cyclotron-produced, allowing distribution and higher resolution).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the two main clinical indications for PSMA PET?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: High-risk primary staging (detecting nodal/bone metastases with higher sensitivity than CT and bone scan) and biochemical recurrence after treatment (localising disease at low PSA when conventional imaging is negative).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List common sites of physiological PSMA uptake that can be misread.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Salivary and lacrimal glands
  • kidneys and ureters
  • liver and spleen
  • small bowel
  • and the urinary bladder (excreted tracer)
Coeliac/sympathetic ganglia are a classic false-positive pitfall.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does PSMA PET link to theranostics?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The same PSMA target used for ⁶⁸Ga/¹⁸F imaging is targeted therapeutically by ¹⁷⁷Lu-PSMA, a beta-emitting radioligand therapy. A PSMA-avid scan confirms the target and selects patients for treatment.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What receptor does ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE bind, and on what tumours is it overexpressed?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It binds somatostatin receptors, chiefly SSTR2, which are overexpressed on well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumours (NETs).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which older scan has ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT largely replaced, and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ¹¹¹In-Octreotide (OctreoScan) SPECT. DOTATATE PET offers higher SSTR2 affinity, better spatial resolution, greater sensitivity and a same-day study.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why and how are somatostatin analogues managed before a DOTATATE scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Octreotide/lanreotide compete for SSTR and can cause false-negatives. Withhold short-acting octreotide ~24h before; scan long-acting depot just before the next dose (~3–4 weeks after the last).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the sites of physiological ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE uptake.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Spleen (usually most intense)
  • adrenals
  • pituitary
  • kidneys/urinary tract
  • liver
  • and the uncinate process of the pancreas (a classic pseudolesion)

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How do DOTATATE and FDG-PET differ across NET grades?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Well-differentiated low-grade NETs are DOTATATE-avid but FDG-negative. High-grade/poorly-differentiated NETs lose SSTR and become FDG-avid but DOTATATE-negative — the flip-flop phenomenon.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: A staging FDG-PET shows an unexpected FDG-avid focus that would make a cancer inoperable. What must you do before withholding curative treatment?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Confirm it histologically (biopsy) where feasible. FDG-PET has false positives (infection, inflammation, brown fat), so a single distant focus should be tissue-proven before a patient is downgraded from curative surgery/radiotherapy to palliation. Positive staging findings go to the MDT.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: FDG-PET confirms active cardiac sarcoidosis. What are the management implications?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Immunosuppression (corticosteroids ± steroid-sparing agents) for active inflammation, and consideration of an ICD/pacemaker because active cardiac sarcoid with high-grade AV block or VT carries a sudden-death risk. Repeat FDG-PET is used to monitor the response to steroids.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the physical basis of SPECT and its key advantage over planar imaging?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A gamma camera rotates 360° around the patient, and projections are reconstructed into 3D tomographic slices of a single-photon emitter (usually ⁹⁹ᵐTc). This removes structure overlap, and SPECT/CT hybrids add anatomical localisation and attenuation correction.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Mechanism of localisation of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP on a bone scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: MDP (methylene diphosphonate) adsorbs onto hydroxyapatite at sites of active bone turnover, so uptake reflects osteoblastic activity and regional blood flow — highlighting mets, fractures, Paget's and infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is a 'superscan' and the 'flare phenomenon'?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Superscan: diffuse intense skeletal uptake with faint/absent kidney and bladder activity, from widespread osteoblastic mets or metabolic bone disease. Flare: apparent worsening of hot spots early after effective treatment, representing healing (osteoblastic) response, not progression.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What tracer is used for a HIDA scan and how does it work?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled iminodiacetic acid analogue — taken up by hepatocytes and excreted unchanged into bile, mapping the biliary tree in real time from liver to duodenum.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What HIDA finding indicates acute cholecystitis, and what other indications exist?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Non-filling of the gallbladder at 60 min (cystic duct obstruction) despite tracer reaching the bowel. HIDA is also used for suspected bile leak (post-cholecystectomy) and neonatal biliary atresia (hepatic uptake but no bowel activity).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which bone-avid tracers are used to image cardiac ATTR, and where?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DPD (UK/Europe), ⁹⁹ᵐTc-PYP (US), and ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMDP. All are bone-seeking diphosphonate/pyrophosphate tracers that bind amyloid microcalcification in ATTR-infiltrated myocardium.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why does the scan distinguish ATTR from AL amyloidosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Bone-avid tracers show intense myocardial uptake in ATTR but characteristically little or none in AL. AL can occasionally take up tracer, so a monoclonal protein screen is still mandatory before diagnosing ATTR.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Describe the Perugini visual grading scale.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Grade 0 = no cardiac uptake (negative)
  • Grade 1 = cardiac < bone (equivocal)
  • Grade 2 = cardiac = bone (positive)
  • Grade 3 = cardiac > bone with reduced bone signal (positive)
Grade 2–3 is positive for ATTR.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What must be checked BEFORE a positive scan can be called ATTR?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Exclusion of AL amyloid with serum free light chains (normal kappa:lambda ratio) plus serum AND urine immunofixation (no monoclonal band). Any abnormality mandates haematology referral and biopsy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which clinical features should prompt bone scintigraphy for ATTR?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Unexplained LVH/HFpEF in an older patient
  • low-voltage ECG despite a thick-walled ventricle (voltage–mass mismatch)
  • and a history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, or biceps tendon rupture

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which radiopharmaceutical is used in three-phase bone scintigraphy and how does it localise?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled diphosphonate (MDP). It is chemisorbed onto hydroxyapatite crystal at sites of active osteoblastic bone mineralisation, so uptake reflects local bone turnover and blood flow.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name the three phases and their timing.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• 1) Flow/angiographic — dynamic over the first ~60s (blood flow)
  • 2) Blood-pool/soft-tissue — immediate static at ~5 min (hyperaemia)
  • 3) Delayed bone phase — static at 2–4h (osteoblastic uptake)

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does osteomyelitis differ from cellulitis on a three-phase scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Osteomyelitis is positive (focal increased uptake) in all three phases. Cellulitis increases flow and blood-pool activity but shows no focal uptake on the delayed bone phase — the delayed phase is the key discriminator.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When is three-phase bone scintigraphy least specific, and what helps?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Specificity falls with recent surgery, fracture, orthopaedic metalwork or a neuropathic (Charcot) joint, all of which raise bone turnover. A labelled white-cell scan (⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO or ¹¹¹In leucocytes), often with a marrow study, improves specificity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Give the main safety points for ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP bone scintigraphy.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Effective dose is a few mSv. Avoid in pregnancy unless justified; minimise close contact and follow local guidance if breastfeeding. Hydrate and void frequently to lower bladder radiation dose.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why can a bone scan be normal in a patient with extensive myeloma or lytic metastases?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A Tc-99m MDP bone scan images osteoBLASTIC (bone-forming) activity. Purely lytic/osteoclastic disease — classically multiple myeloma (and some aggressive lytic mets) — produces little osteoblastic reaction, so it is photopenic (cold) / falsely negative. Image myeloma with whole-body MRI, CT or a skeletal survey, not a bone scan.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which radiopharmaceutical is preferred for a dynamic renogram and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAG3 — it is actively secreted by the proximal tubules with high extraction, giving superior image quality, especially in kidneys with poor function. ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA (glomerular filtration) is the alternative.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does the F+20 / frusemide diuretic renogram distinguish?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: True mechanical obstruction (rising curve that does NOT wash out after diuretic) from a baggy, dilated but non-obstructed system (prompt washout after frusemide).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Describe the normal renogram curve.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A rapid rise (uptake), a peak at about 3–5 minutes, then a steady fall as tracer is excreted and drains to the bladder.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is captopril used in renography, and what does a positive study show?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Captopril (an ACE inhibitor) unmasks a functionally significant renal artery stenosis. A positive study shows worsening of the affected kidney's curve after captopril — delayed time-to-peak, delayed excretion and reduced relative uptake versus baseline.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name two patient-prep factors that can cause a false non-washout (false obstruction) pattern.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Dehydration (slows tracer transit) and a full bladder causing back-pressure — so hydrate the patient and have them void before imaging.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the mechanism of localisation of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It is taken up and fixed in proximal renal tubular cells of the cortex, with minimal collecting-system excretion, so uptake maps functioning cortical mass.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is DMSA the best test for split renal function and scarring?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Because retained cortical tracer directly reflects viable functioning parenchyma, giving high-resolution cortical images and accurate differential (split) function without pelvicalyceal activity obscuring the cortex.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How do you distinguish acute pyelonephritis from a chronic scar on DMSA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Acute pyelonephritis shows photopenic (cold) defects with a preserved renal outline and no volume loss; a scar shows a focal defect with cortical thinning/volume loss, classically wedge-shaped.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When should scarring be assessed on DMSA relative to an acute UTI?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Delayed several months (usually at least 4–6 months) after the acute infection, so acute inflammatory change is not mistaken for a permanent scar.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When is DMSA imaging performed after injection, and what is a normal split function?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Imaging is performed about 2–4 hours after IV injection; normal split function is roughly symmetrical, around 45–55% per kidney.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate localise in the thyroid, and what is its key limitation?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It is trapped by the sodium-iodide symporter but NOT organified. It therefore reflects trapping only and cannot assess organification defects (unlike radioiodine).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Thyrotoxic patient with diffuse, homogeneously increased tracer uptake across an enlarged gland — diagnosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Graves' disease.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Single hot nodule with suppressed uptake in the surrounding gland — diagnosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Toxic (autonomously functioning) adenoma.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Thyrotoxic patient with near-absent thyroid uptake — differential?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Thyroiditis (de Quervain's, silent/post-partum)
  • factitious thyrotoxicosis
  • iodine load
  • or recent amiodarone

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does a COLD (hypofunctioning) nodule imply and what is the next step?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A slightly higher malignancy risk than a hot nodule — proceed to ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does the thyroid concentrate radioiodine, and why does this make iodine isotopes useful both diagnostically and therapeutically?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Follicular cells trap iodide via the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) and organify it into thyroid hormone. Gamma-emitting ¹²³I images this uptake (RAIU), while beta-emitting ¹³¹I delivers a local ablative dose to functioning tissue for therapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: In a thyrotoxic patient, what do HIGH versus LOW radioiodine uptake indicate?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: High uptake = Graves' disease (diffuse) or toxic nodular disease / toxic adenoma (focal). Low uptake = thyroiditis (subacute, postpartum), iodine load (contrast, amiodarone), or factitious thyroxine ingestion.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Contrast ¹²³I and ¹³¹I in terms of emission, half-life and use.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ¹²³I: pure gamma emitter, ~13 h half-life, low dose — used for diagnostic uptake and imaging. ¹³¹I: beta and gamma emitter, ~8 day half-life — beta particles ablate tissue for therapy of hyperthyroidism and thyroid cancer, and it is used for whole-body scans.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the absolute contraindications and key post-therapy precautions for ¹³¹I radioiodine?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications (mandatory pregnancy test first). After therapy:
  • keep distance from children and pregnant women
  • limit close contact
  • and avoid pregnancy for about 6 months

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why must patients follow a low-iodine diet and stop antithyroid drugs before radioiodine, and what is a risk in Graves' patients?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Iodine loading and antithyroid drugs suppress uptake, reducing efficacy, so both are stopped/avoided beforehand. In Graves' disease, radioiodine can precipitate or worsen thyroid eye disease, especially in smokers, sometimes needing steroid cover.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the purpose of ultrasound guidance during thyroid FNA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It directs the needle into the most suspicious solid, vascular part of the nodule and avoids cystic/necrotic areas, improving sample adequacy and reducing non-diagnostic (Thy1) results compared with palpation-guided FNA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What do Thy1 and Thy1c mean, and what is the next step?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Thy1 = non-diagnostic/inadequate; Thy1c = cystic non-diagnostic (acellular cyst fluid). Management is to repeat the US-guided FNA, sampling any solid component.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why can't cytology (Thy3f) distinguish a follicular adenoma from a follicular carcinoma?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The malignant diagnosis depends on capsular and vascular invasion, which is an architectural feature. FNA samples loose cells only, so it cannot assess the capsule — a diagnostic hemithyroidectomy is needed for histology.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does the BTA 'U' ultrasound classification (U1-U5) represent?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
A sonographic risk score:
  • U1 normal
  • U2 benign
  • U3 indeterminate
  • U4 suspicious
  • U5 malignant
U3-U5 nodules are selected for FNA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How is a Thy2 benign cytology managed, and what is the key caveat?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Thy2 (non-neoplastic/benign, e.g. colloid nodule) is managed by reassurance and discharge or interval ultrasound. Caveat: a benign result must not override a suspicious ultrasound or clinical features — discordance needs MDT review and re-sampling.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What three tracer properties make an ideal GFR marker, and which isotopes are used?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Freely filtered at the glomerulus, not secreted, and not reabsorbed by the tubules — so plasma clearance equals GFR. UK tracers are ⁵¹Cr-EDTA (chromium-51) or ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Outline the isotope GFR method.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Single accurately-measured IV bolus of tracer, then timed venous blood samples (e.g. 2, 3, 4 h) from the opposite arm. Log plasma activity is plotted against time; the terminal slope/AUC gives clearance, corrected to body surface area (mL/min/1.73m²).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is isotope GFR preferred over creatinine-based eGFR?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It directly measures filtration of a pure marker rather than estimating from creatinine, which depends on muscle mass. It is the reference/gold-standard when accuracy changes management — chemo dosing, kidney donors, children, and extremes of muscle mass or amputees.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which chemotherapy dosing formula relies on an accurate measured GFR?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The Calvert formula for carboplatin: dose = target AUC × (GFR + 25). An isotope GFR is requested to avoid over- or under-dosing this nephrotoxic drug.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What clinical state most distorts an isotope GFR result, and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Extracellular fluid overload (oedema, ascites): the tracer distributes into the expanded ECF, delaying equilibration and giving an unreliable single-pool result. Extended/multi-sample protocols are needed. Accurate dose and sample timing are also essential.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: A MAG3 renogram shows a rising curve that does not wash out after frusemide (F+20). What does this mean and what is done?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It confirms true mechanical obstruction (a dilated but non-obstructed ‘baggy’ system would wash out with frusemide). Action: refer urology, decompress the kidney (percutaneous nephrostomy or JJ stent) and treat the cause — e.g. pyeloplasty for PUJ obstruction — and monitor split function.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does a thyroid isotope scan change management of a hot versus a cold nodule?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A hot (autonomous) nodule takes up tracer with the rest of the gland suppressed — almost always benign; treat hyperthyroidism (radioiodine/surgery), not FNA. A cold nodule is non-functioning with a ~10–20% malignancy risk → ultrasound + FNA (Thy grading). Isotope scans are used mainly when TSH is low (to find the cause of thyrotoxicosis).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which two radiopharmaceuticals are used in a V/Q scan and by what route?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Perfusion: IV ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA (macroaggregated albumin), which lodges in pulmonary capillaries. Ventilation: inhaled ⁹⁹ᵐTc-Technegas or ⁸¹ᵐKr gas reaching the alveoli.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the diagnostic hallmark of PE on a V/Q scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A MISMATCH — a perfusion defect with preserved (normal) ventilation in the same lung region. Matched V and Q defects point to airway/parenchymal disease instead.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When is a V/Q scan preferred over CTPA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
Suspected PE with a NORMAL chest X-ray in patients where CTPA is contraindicated or best avoided:
  • contrast allergy
  • renal impairment
  • or to reduce breast radiation in younger women and pregnancy

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does a normal perfusion scan tell you about PE?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A normal perfusion scan effectively excludes pulmonary embolism.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How is a V/Q scan reported?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: By probability (PIOPED-style): normal, low, intermediate/indeterminate, or high probability. High probability requires large mismatched segmental perfusion defects.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does uptake of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-sestamibi/tetrofosmin in the myocardium reflect?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Regional coronary blood flow AND myocyte viability — the lipophilic cation is trapped in mitochondria of perfused, living myocytes in proportion to flow.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Reversible vs fixed defect on SPECT MPI — meaning?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Reversible (abnormal on stress, normal at rest) = inducible ischaemia from a flow-limiting stenosis. Fixed (abnormal on both) = infarct/scar (non-viable), though hibernating myocardium can mimic it.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How do vasodilator stress agents (adenosine/dipyridamole/regadenoson) reveal ischaemia?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: They dilate normal coronaries but stenosed vessels are already maximally dilated, creating flow heterogeneity/'coronary steal' so diseased territories show relatively reduced tracer uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Key contraindications and prep for adenosine/dipyridamole MPI stress?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Contraindicated in asthma/bronchospasm and high-grade AV block (no pacemaker). Withhold caffeine and theophylline ≥12–24 h (competitive antagonists causing false negatives). Have resuscitation facilities and aminophylline ready.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which stress agent is preferred when a patient has asthma, and why choose it?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Dobutamine — an inotrope/chronotrope that raises myocardial oxygen demand rather than acting on adenosine receptors, so it avoids the bronchospasm risk of vasodilators.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: By what mechanism does MIBG localise to tumours?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: MIBG is a noradrenaline (norepinephrine) analogue taken up via the noradrenaline transporter into adrenergic/sympathomedullary and neural-crest tissue, then stored in neurosecretory granules.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the main indications for an MIBG scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Localising and staging phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma
  • and neuroblastoma in children
  • also assessing avidity/suitability for 131I-MIBG therapy

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why and how is thyroid blockade given before an MIBG scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Potassium iodide or Lugol's iodine is given before and after the scan to saturate the thyroid and block uptake of free radioiodine, protecting the gland from radiation. Blockade is longer when 131I is used.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which drugs must be withheld before MIBG imaging and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Labetalol (and other combined alpha/beta blockers), tricyclic antidepressants, sympathomimetics/decongestants and some calcium-channel blockers block or displace MIBG at the noradrenaline transporter, causing false-negative scans.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When are images acquired and what are the normal physiological uptake sites?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
Imaging at 24 hours, with delayed 48-hour views if needed, often with SPECT/CT. Physiological uptake:
  • salivary glands
  • myocardium
  • liver
  • spleen
  • bowel and bladder

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does ¹²³I-ioflupane (DaTscan) bind, and where?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The presynaptic dopamine transporter (DAT) on nigrostriatal dopaminergic nerve terminals in the striatum (caudate nucleus and putamen).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What appearance is normal vs abnormal on a DaTscan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Normal = symmetric crescent/'comma'-shaped uptake in both striata. Abnormal = reduced/asymmetric uptake shrinking to a 'full stop'/period and losing the putaminal tail (presynaptic dopaminergic deficit).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which conditions give a REDUCED DaTscan vs a NORMAL one?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Reduced (degenerative): Parkinson's disease, MSA, PSP, and dementia with Lewy bodies. Normal (intact terminals): essential tremor, drug-induced, vascular and psychogenic parkinsonism.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the key limitation of a DaTscan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It confirms a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit but CANNOT distinguish Parkinson's disease from MSA or PSP, since all degenerative parkinsonian syndromes reduce striatal uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What patient preparation is required before a DaTscan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Thyroid blockade with potassium iodide/perchlorate to protect the thyroid from free radioiodide, and withholding drugs that affect DAT binding (cocaine, some stimulants such as methylphenidate/amfetamine, and certain antidepressants like bupropion). SPECT imaging is performed ~3–6 hours after injection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which radiopharmaceutical is used for labelled RBC scintigraphy in GI bleeding, and where does it localise?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled autologous red blood cells. They remain in the intravascular blood pool; extravasation into the bowel lumen produces an abnormal focus of activity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the diagnostic hallmark of a positive labelled RBC bleeding scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A focus of activity that appears, increases in intensity, and moves along the bowel with peristalsis on dynamic imaging.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What bleeding rate can labelled RBC scintigraphy detect, and how does this compare to angiography?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: As low as ~0.1–0.4 mL/min — more sensitive than CT angiography or catheter angiography, which need faster bleeding.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Give the main advantage and the main limitation of labelled RBC scintigraphy.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Advantage: prolonged/repeatable imaging window catches slow, intermittent bleeds. Limitation: localises the region but not the exact cause, and peristalsis can mislocalise the source.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does the Meckel's scan differ from labelled RBC scintigraphy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It uses free ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate (not RBC-bound), which is taken up by ectopic gastric mucosa in a Meckel's diverticulum — a classic cause of painless PR bleeding in children.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How do labelled white cells localise to infection?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Autologous leucocytes (mainly neutrophils) are labelled ex vivo and reinjected; they marginate, extravasate and accumulate at sites of active neutrophilic inflammation in response to chemotactic signals, so uptake marks active infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Compare ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO and ¹¹¹In-oxine for leucocyte labelling.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO gives lower dose and sharper images but shows physiological bowel/urinary/gallbladder clearance on delayed views. ¹¹¹In-oxine is very stable with no bowel excretion (good for abdominal sepsis) but delivers a higher dose with poorer resolution.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why add a bone marrow scan to a labelled WCC scan for prosthetic joint infection?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Normal/displaced marrow takes up leucocytes and can mimic infection. Infection is WCC uptake that is NOT matched on the marrow map (incongruent); congruent uptake is marrow. This co-registration greatly improves specificity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What imaging pattern over time indicates active infection on a labelled WCC scan?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A focus of uptake outside the normal liver/spleen/marrow distribution that is stable or increases in intensity and extent between early and delayed images indicates active infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the main indications for a labelled white cell scan.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Suspected osteomyelitis (especially prosthetic joint infection and diabetic foot)
  • infected vascular grafts
  • occult abdominal/pelvic collections
  • inflammatory bowel disease activity
  • and pyrexia/inflammation of unknown origin

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the sentinel lymph node?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The first lymph node (or nodes) into which a tumour drains, and therefore the first likely site of nodal metastasis. Its status is used to predict the state of the whole regional nodal basin.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which radiopharmaceutical is used for sentinel node mapping and how does it localise?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled nanocolloid, injected around the tumour or biopsy site. The small colloid particles enter the lymphatics and are trapped/phagocytosed in the first draining (sentinel) node, making it a focal hot spot on gamma imaging.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is 'dual localisation' in sentinel node biopsy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Combining the radiotracer (⁹⁹ᵐTc-nanocolloid, found with the gamma probe) with intra-operative blue dye that stains the node and afferent lymphatic blue. Using both raises the sentinel-node identification rate above either method alone.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What do a negative and a positive sentinel node each mean for management?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A negative sentinel node avoids the need for full axillary/regional nodal dissection, sparing the patient its morbidity (lymphoedema). A positive node guides further management such as further nodal treatment, radiotherapy or surveillance.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name the key safety issues in sentinel node lymphoscintigraphy.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Low radiation dose from the small ⁹⁹ᵐTc activity (safe for patient and staff)
  • risk of anaphylaxis to patent blue dye plus transient blue staining and an artefactual SpO₂ drop
  • pregnancy is a relative contraindication and breastfeeding may need temporary interruption

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: A positive MIBG scan localises a phaeochromocytoma. What is the management sequence?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Definitive treatment is surgical resection, but the patient must first be blocked pharmacologically: ALPHA-blockade first (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) to control BP, THEN beta-blockade. Giving a beta-blocker before alpha-blockade risks unopposed alpha vasoconstriction → hypertensive crisis. Ensure volume repletion pre-operatively.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When is a V/Q scan preferred over CTPA for PE, and what does a high-probability scan mean?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: V/Q is preferred when CTPA is contraindicated/undesirable: contrast allergy, renal impairment, or a young woman/pregnancy (lower maternal breast dose; a normal CXR helps). A high-probability scan (≥2 large mismatched perfusion defects with normal ventilation) means treat for PE (anticoagulate); a normal perfusion scan effectively excludes PE.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the two broad indications for peripheral angioplasty in PAD?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Lifestyle-limiting intermittent claudication refractory to conservative therapy, and critical limb-threatening ischaemia (rest pain, ulceration or gangrene).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Antegrade vs retrograde common femoral access — when is each used?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Retrograde (often up-and-over) accesses contralateral iliac/femoral disease; antegrade access is used for ipsilateral femoropopliteal and infrapopliteal (below-knee) lesions.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What does the TASC classification describe and how does it guide treatment?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It grades lesions A–D by length, number and complexity. A/B favour endovascular therapy, D favours surgical bypass, and C is decided case-by-case.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which type of stent suits the mobile femoropopliteal segment and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Self-expanding stents, because they tolerate flexion and compression; balloon-mounted stents are reserved for sites needing precise placement such as the iliac ostium.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the key antiplatelet regimen around peripheral stenting?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Aspirin is continued, with clopidogrel added (dual antiplatelet therapy) for a defined period after stenting, then usually lifelong single-agent antiplatelet therapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the angiographic hallmark of active arterial bleeding on DSA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Focal contrast extravasation (a 'blush') that pools and persists beyond the arterial phase into the venous phase. It marks the bleeding point and is the target for embolisation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which embolic agent is temporary, and why is that useful in trauma and post-partum haemorrhage?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Gelfoam (gelatin sponge) resorbs over days, allowing vessel recanalisation and tissue recovery once haemostasis is achieved, reducing the risk of permanent end-organ infarction.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is 'empirical' (blind) embolisation?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Embolising the vessel/territory identified as the culprit on CT even when no active blush is seen at DSA (bleeding may be intermittent). Common in localised GI bleeds and epistaxis (sphenopalatine artery).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Distinguish proximal from distal embolisation in the spleen.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Proximal (main splenic artery coiling) lowers perfusion pressure while collaterals preserve the spleen; distal/superselective embolisation targets the exact bleeding segment but carries a higher risk of focal splenic infarction.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is post-embolisation syndrome?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A self-limiting cluster of pain, low-grade fever, nausea and raised inflammatory markers over the days after embolisation, caused by tissue ischaemia. Managed with analgesia and supportive care, not antibiotics.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the mechanism by which UAE treats fibroids?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Embolic particles (PVA or calibrated microspheres) are injected into both uterine arteries to occlude the fibroid blood supply, causing fibroid infarction and shrinkage while collateral flow spares the myometrium/uterus.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the two main symptom groups that indicate UAE for fibroids?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding with anaemia) and bulk/pressure symptoms (pelvic pain, urinary frequency, mass effect/distension).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is post-embolisation syndrome and how is it managed?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: An expected, self-limiting reaction after UAE: crampy pelvic pain, low-grade fever, nausea and malaise. Managed supportively with strong analgesia (often PCA), NSAIDs and antiemetics, not antibiotics.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the key angiographic findings during UAE?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Hypertrophied, tortuous, enlarged uterine arteries and a hypervascular fibroid "blush". The endpoint is near-stasis with loss of the fibroid blush; both uterine arteries must be treated.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is myomectomy generally preferred over UAE when fertility is desired?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: UAE carries a risk of non-target embolisation of the ovarian supply, reducing ovarian reserve and fertility and potentially causing premature ovarian failure; myomectomy better preserves fertility.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why do transarterial liver therapies (TACE/TARE) work selectively on tumour?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Normal liver is supplied mainly by the portal vein (~75%), whereas HCC and hypervascular metastases derive their blood supply predominantly from the hepatic artery. Delivering agents into the hepatic artery concentrates them in tumour while sparing normal parenchyma.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the standard indication for TACE in HCC?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Intermediate-stage (BCLC B) HCC: multinodular disease with preserved liver function (Child-Pugh A or well-compensated B) and no macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread, not suitable for resection, transplant or ablation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What pre-treatment work-up is unique to TARE (Y-90)?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A mapping angiogram with 99mTc-MAA to measure the lung shunt fraction (predicting radiation pneumonitis risk) and to detect GI non-target flow, allowing prophylactic coil embolisation of aberrant vessels before the therapeutic dose.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is post-embolisation syndrome?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The commonest complication after TACE: self-limiting fever, right-upper-quadrant pain, nausea and malaise over the following days, managed supportively with analgesia, antiemetics and fluids.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why might TARE be chosen over TACE in a patient with portal vein thrombosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Y-90 radioembolisation is minimally embolic and kills by internal beta radiation rather than ischaemia, so it is safer when portal inflow is already compromised, whereas the ischaemic insult of TACE risks liver decompensation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: In catheter-directed thrombolysis, how is the thrombolytic delivered to the clot?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A multi-side-hole catheter is positioned within the thrombus under fluoroscopy and a thrombolytic (e.g. alteplase/tPA) is infused directly into the clot, usually over hours with repeat venography, ± pharmacomechanical or aspiration thrombectomy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the single most important complication of thrombolytic therapy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Major bleeding, with intracranial haemorrhage being the feared catastrophic event. Careful patient selection and fibrinogen monitoring reduce this risk.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which blood parameter is monitored during a thrombolysis infusion, and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Fibrinogen. A marked fall (e.g. below ~1 g/L) indicates systemic fibrinolysis and heightened bleeding risk, prompting reduction or cessation of lysis.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name key contraindications to catheter-directed thrombolysis.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Active internal bleeding
  • recent haemorrhagic or ischaemic stroke
  • recent major surgery or trauma
  • intracranial tumour/vascular malformation
  • and uncontrolled hypertension

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is catheter-directed thrombolysis considered for extensive iliofemoral DVT in selected younger patients?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: To reduce the risk of post-thrombotic syndrome by clearing extensive proximal clot, reserved for younger patients with good function and low bleeding risk.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why are varicoceles usually left-sided?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The left gonadal (testicular) vein drains into the left renal vein at a near right angle, giving a higher venous pressure and longer column, which promotes reflux. The right gonadal vein drains obliquely and directly into the IVC.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the main indications for varicocele embolisation?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Symptomatic varicocele causing scrotal pain/dragging ache, or subfertility with impaired semen parameters. Pre-procedure work-up includes scrotal Doppler ultrasound to confirm reflux.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Outline the technique of gonadal vein embolisation.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Ultrasound-guided venous access (usually right internal jugular or common femoral vein)
  • selective catheterisation of the gonadal vein
  • venography to confirm reflux
  • then occlusion with coils plus or minus sclerosant
  • followed by completion venography

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the female equivalent of varicocele embolisation and its indication?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Ovarian vein embolisation for pelvic congestion syndrome: chronic pelvic pain with vulvar/pelvic varices, typically in multiparous women.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List key complications of gonadal vein embolisation.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Coil migration (e.g. to pulmonary circulation)
  • non-target embolisation
  • gonadal vein perforation
  • recurrence via collaterals
  • contrast reaction
  • and radiation (gonadal dose, generally low/acceptable)

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the two core indications for an IVC filter?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Proven VTE (DVT/PE) with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation, or recurrent PE despite adequate therapeutic anticoagulation. (Prophylaxis in selected very high-risk trauma/peri-operative patients is a more controversial third use.)

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: At what level in the IVC is a filter normally deployed, and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: In the infrarenal IVC, just below the lowest renal vein. This preserves renal venous drainage above the device if the filter thromboses. Suprarenal placement is reserved for special cases such as thrombus extending above the renal veins or pregnancy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why should retrievable IVC filters be removed promptly?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: They should be removed once anticoagulation can be safely started or the high-risk period passes. Retained filters accumulate complications (tilt, penetration, fracture, IVC occlusion) and become progressively harder to retrieve as they endothelialise.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is checked on cavography before filter deployment?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• IVC patency and absence of thrombus at the deployment site
  • the IVC diameter (most filters certified to ~28–30 mm)
  • and the position of the renal vein ostia to guide infrarenal placement

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the main complications of IVC filters.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Filter migration
  • IVC penetration/perforation
  • filter thrombosis with IVC occlusion
  • strut fracture/fragment embolisation
  • increased recurrent DVT
  • and failure to retrieve

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Where should the tip of a central venous catheter sit?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: At the cavoatrial junction (SVC/right atrium border). Too high risks thrombosis; too far into the right atrium risks arrhythmia and perforation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the purpose of the Dacron cuff in a tunnelled (Hickman) line?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It sits in the subcutaneous tunnel and promotes fibrous tissue ingrowth, which anchors the catheter and acts as a mechanical barrier reducing ascending infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which central venous access device has the lowest infection rate and best cosmesis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The totally implantable port (subcutaneous reservoir accessed by a non-coring Huber needle) — ideal for intermittent long-term chemotherapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What coagulation thresholds are typically required before central line insertion?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L and INR ≤ 1.5; correct abnormalities and review/hold anticoagulants and antiplatelets per local protocol first.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What imaging is used during and immediately after image-guided central line placement?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Real-time ultrasound for venous puncture
  • fluoroscopy to confirm guidewire/tip at the cavoatrial junction
  • and a post-procedure CXR to confirm position and exclude pneumothorax

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the first-line management for an accessible infected intra-abdominal collection?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Image-guided percutaneous catheter drainage (under US or CT guidance), preferred over open surgery when a safe access window exists.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Describe the Seldinger technique for abscess drainage.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Fine needle into the collection
  • pass a guidewire
  • serially dilate the tract over the wire
  • then railroad a locking pigtail catheter into position

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What coagulation thresholds are typically required before percutaneous drainage?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: INR ≤ 1.5 and platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L; correct coagulopathy and hold anticoagulants/antiplatelets beforehand.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When can an abscess drainage catheter be removed?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: When output falls below about 10–20 mL/day, the patient is clinically improving, and follow-up imaging confirms the collection has resolved.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What adjunct is used for a loculated empyema that drains poorly?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Intrapleural fibrinolytics — tPA combined with DNase — to break down septations and reduce fluid viscosity, improving drainage and often avoiding surgery.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the classic emergency indication for percutaneous nephrostomy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: An obstructed AND infected collecting system (pyonephrosis) — a urological emergency requiring urgent decompression, as antibiotics alone cannot clear pus behind an obstruction.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which calyx is targeted during percutaneous nephrostomy and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A posterior lower-pole calyx. The posterior calyx lies in the relatively avascular plane (line of Brödel) minimising bleeding, and the lower-pole route stays below the pleura, avoiding pneumothorax.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What imaging guidance is used for PCN and how is access confirmed?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Combined ultrasound (for the initial puncture) and fluoroscopy. Access is confirmed by aspirating urine and injecting contrast (nephrostogram) before passing a guidewire, dilating the track, and deploying a locking pigtail catheter.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is an antegrade ureteric stent and when is it used?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A double-J stent passed down the ureter into the bladder via nephrostomy access, used to internalise drainage across an obstruction (e.g. malignant stricture or stone), especially when retrograde stenting has failed.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the main complications of percutaneous nephrostomy.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Bleeding/haematuria (AV fistula or pseudoaneurysm from the vascular kidney)
  • sepsis (draining an infected system)
  • injury to bowel or pleura (pneumothorax with upper-pole puncture)
  • and tube dislodgement/blockage

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When is percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage (PTBD) preferred over ERCP?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
When ERCP has failed or is not possible — e.g.
  • altered anatomy (Roux-en-Y, previous gastrectomy)
  • an inaccessible papilla
  • or high hilar (Klatskin) strictures
Also for urgent decompression of an obstructed, infected system.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why must coagulation be corrected before PTC/PTBD, and how?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Obstructive jaundice causes fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption, prolonging the INR. The transhepatic tract crosses vascular liver, risking bleeding/haemobilia. Give IV vitamin K ± FFP/platelets; aim INR ≤ 1.5 and platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Outline the essential technique steps of PTBD.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: US/fluoro-guided fine-needle puncture of a peripheral bile duct → contrast cholangiogram to define anatomy/level of obstruction → guidewire across the stricture → tract dilatation → placement of external, internal-external, or stented (SEMS/plastic) drain.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the main complications of PTC/PTBD.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Bleeding and haemobilia (hepatic artery/portal vein injury)
  • sepsis/cholangitis
  • bile leak causing bile peritonitis
  • pneumothorax from intercostal puncture
  • and tube problems (blockage, dislodgement, pericatheter leak)

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why are prophylactic antibiotics essential in biliary intervention?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The obstructed biliary tree is frequently colonised/infected, and instrumentation with contrast injection causes bacteraemia and can precipitate cholangitis and sepsis. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics are given before the procedure.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is a RIG and what imaging guides it?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Radiologically-inserted gastrostomy: placement of a feeding tube through the anterior abdominal wall into the stomach for long-term enteral feeding, performed under fluoroscopic guidance.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why choose RIG over PEG in an obstructing head & neck / oesophageal tumour?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The tumour prevents passage of the endoscope needed for a PEG. RIG uses fluoroscopy and an NG tube to distend the stomach, so no endoscope has to pass the obstruction.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why may an MND patient tolerate RIG better than PEG?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: MND patients often have poor respiratory reserve (low FVC). RIG avoids endoscopy and deep sedation, so it is safer than sedation-requiring PEG; gastrostomy should ideally precede further respiratory decline.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is gastropexy in RIG and why is it done?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: T-fasteners (retention sutures) anchor the stomach to the abdominal wall, apposing the two surfaces. This reduces the risk of intraperitoneal leak and peritonitis and secures the tract.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List the key pre-procedure checks before a RIG.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Check and correct coagulation (INR, platelets, hold anticoagulants/antiplatelets)
  • assess aspiration risk
  • ensure fasting
  • give antibiotic prophylaxis
  • obtain consent
  • and confirm the MDT/nutrition decision

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the workhorse device for endovascular foreign body retrieval, and what does it need to work best?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The loop (gooseneck) snare. It works best when a free end of the foreign body lies free within the vessel lumen, allowing the loop to be passed over it, tightened and withdrawn through a sheath. Forceps and basket devices are alternatives when no free end is snareable.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why should retained intravascular foreign bodies (e.g. a sheared catheter fragment) be retrieved even if asymptomatic?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
They risk
  • thrombosis
  • sepsis
  • cardiac arrhythmia
  • valve or chamber perforation
  • and pulmonary embolism
Because of these serious complications, retrieval is recommended rather than leaving the fragment in situ.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the usual vascular access for retrieving an embolised catheter fragment from the great veins or right heart?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Ultrasound-guided right common femoral vein puncture, giving a large-calibre straight route to the SVC and right heart, with a generously sized sheath to allow the captured fragment to be withdrawn. Internal jugular access is an alternative.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name a classic cause of a fractured, centrally-migrated port (Portacath) catheter.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Pinch-off syndrome: the catheter is compressed between the clavicle and first rib, fractures at that point, and the distal fragment embolises centrally to the SVC, right atrium or pulmonary artery.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What pre-procedure coagulation targets apply before endovascular foreign body retrieval?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Correct significant coagulopathy first: aim for INR of about 1.5 or less and platelets of at least 50 × 10⁹/L, and review anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy, alongside consent and imaging localisation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: FNA vs core biopsy — which for solid tumour typing, and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Core biopsy (histology): a wider cutting needle yields a tissue core that preserves architecture and allows immunohistochemistry and molecular markers. FNA gives only cells (cytology) and does not preserve architecture.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which imaging guidance for a superficial vascular lesion vs a deep/lung lesion?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Ultrasound (real-time, colour Doppler to avoid vessels, no radiation) for superficial/vascular targets, liver, kidney and nodes. CT for deep, retroperitoneal, lung and bone lesions.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Key complication of CT-guided lung biopsy and its post-procedure requirement?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Pneumothorax. A post-biopsy chest X-ray (CXR) is done to detect/monitor it before discharge; a large or symptomatic pneumothorax may need aspiration or a chest drain.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What must be checked and corrected before percutaneous biopsy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Coagulation (INR/clotting) and platelet count — correct if deranged — and stop/withhold anticoagulants and antiplatelets (warfarin, DOACs, clopidogrel) per protocol. Also obtain consent and confirm the lesion/approach on imaging.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is coaxial biopsy technique and why is it used?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: A guiding/introducer needle is placed to the lesion edge and the cutting needle passed through it to take multiple cores through a single track. It avoids repeated punctures, reduces bleeding and lowers the risk of tumour track seeding.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: When is transjugular liver biopsy preferred over percutaneous biopsy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
When there is
  • significant coagulopathy
  • thrombocytopenia
  • or ascites (high bleeding risk)
  • or when hepatic venous pressure gradient measurement is also required

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Why is the transjugular route safer in high-bleeding-risk patients?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The needle stays within the vascular system, so any bleeding from the biopsy track drains back into the hepatic vein rather than into the peritoneal cavity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Describe the catheter route in transjugular liver biopsy.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Right internal jugular vein access, then via the superior vena cava to the right atrium to the inferior vena cava and into a (usually right) hepatic vein; the needle is then passed through the vein wall into the parenchyma.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What additional haemodynamic measurement can TJLB provide?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: The hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG), which assesses portal hypertension; a gradient of 10 mmHg or more indicates clinically significant portal hypertension.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Name two complications specific to transjugular liver biopsy.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Cardiac arrhythmia (catheter transiting the right atrium) and neck haematoma/carotid puncture from jugular access; also capsular perforation with bleeding and smaller/fragmented samples.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How does radiofrequency ablation (RFA) destroy tumour tissue?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Alternating current passed through an electrode causes ionic agitation and frictional heating of the tissue, producing coagulative necrosis of the tumour.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the 'heat-sink' effect in thermal tumour ablation?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Blood flowing through a large vessel adjacent to the tumour carries heat away, cooling the tissue and limiting the ablation zone near the vessel. This risks incomplete ablation; microwave ablation is less affected than RFA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Give two advantages of microwave ablation (MWA) over RFA.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: MWA is faster and reaches higher temperatures producing larger ablation zones, and it is less affected by the heat-sink effect, making it better for tumours near large vessels.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which ablation modality is favoured for painful bone metastases and small renal tumours, and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Cryoablation — freeze–thaw cycles cause ice-crystal cell death, it produces a visible ice-ball for monitoring, and it tends to be less painful, making it well suited to bone mets and renal cell carcinoma.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the first-line treatment of choice for osteoid osteoma?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: CT-guided percutaneous radiofrequency ablation (RFA) of the nidus, which reliably relieves the characteristic night pain.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What cement is used in vertebral augmentation, and what is the key difference between vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA). Vertebroplasty injects cement directly via a transpedicular needle; kyphoplasty first inflates a balloon (bone tamp) to create a cavity and partially restore height, then injects cement at lower pressure.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: Which MRI finding confirms an acute vertebral fracture suitable for augmentation?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Marrow oedema (high signal on STIR/T2) within the vertebral body indicates an acute, unhealed fracture likely to respond. MRI also excludes infection and cord compression.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the most feared complication of vertebroplasty and how is it detected intra-procedurally?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Cement leak/extravasation into the spinal canal causing cord or nerve compression. It is detected by real-time (live) fluoroscopy showing cement tracking posteriorly, prompting immediate cessation of injection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: How can cement escaping into paravertebral veins present, and what is that complication?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Pulmonary cement embolism, presenting with dyspnoea, hypoxia or chest pain. It is mitigated by using viscous cement and injecting under continuous live fluoroscopy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: State the key coagulation thresholds and infection rule before vertebral augmentation.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Correct INR to ≤ 1.5 and ensure platelets ≥ 50 × 10⁹/L; hold/bridge anticoagulants. Active spinal infection must be excluded as it is a contraindication.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What two vessels does a TIPS connect, and through what?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: It connects the portal vein to a hepatic vein via a covered stent passed through the liver parenchyma, creating a low-resistance portosystemic shunt to decompress portal hypertension.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What are the two main indications for TIPS?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Refractory or recurrent variceal bleeding (oesophageal/gastric) not controlled by endoscopy plus drugs, and refractory ascites (or hepatic hydrothorax).

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What is the key/defining complication of TIPS and why?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy, because shunted blood bypasses the liver's detoxification, causing hyperammonaemia. It is managed with lactulose/rifaximin.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: What access and target pressure define a TIPS procedure?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back: Right internal jugular access to the hepatic vein, then transparenchymal needle pass into a portal vein branch. The portosystemic gradient is measured and reduced, aiming for <12 mmHg.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.front: List key contraindications to TIPS.
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.back:
• Severe hepatic encephalopathy
  • heart failure/pulmonary hypertension
  • severe liver failure (high MELD)
  • polycystic liver disease
  • and right heart failure

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: What is the biochemical basis for ¹⁸F-FDG retention within tumour cells?
options: It is phosphorylated to FDG-6-phosphate and trapped intracellularly
It binds irreversibly to cell-surface somatostatin receptors
It is incorporated into newly synthesised DNA strands
It chelates intracellular calcium in metabolically active cells
It is actively secreted into the biliary system and reabsorbed
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It is phosphorylated to FDG-6-phosphate and trapped intracellularly
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: FDG enters cells via GLUT transporters and is phosphorylated by hexokinase to FDG-6-phosphate. This charged metabolite cannot progress through glycolysis or be dephosphorylated, so it accumulates in proportion to the cell's glycolytic activity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient is booked for FDG PET-CT. Which preparation instruction is correct?
options: Fast for at least 6 hours and ensure blood glucose is controlled
Perform vigorous exercise on the morning of the scan
Remain in a cold room during the uptake period
Eat a high-carbohydrate meal one hour before injection
Receive a large intravenous dextrose load before injection
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Fast for at least 6 hours and ensure blood glucose is controlled
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Fasting for at least 6 hours lowers insulin and blood glucose so that tumour cells out-compete normal tissue for FDG. Hyperglycaemia competes with the tracer and degrades image quality, so glucose is ideally kept below 11 mmol/L.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which malignancy is most likely to be FDG PET-negative, limiting the test's sensitivity?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Renal cell carcinoma
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma characteristically shows low FDG avidity, and urinary excretion of tracer through the renal tract further obscures assessment. The other listed tumours are typically strongly FDG-avid and well demonstrated on PET-CT.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient is booked for cardiac FDG-PET to assess suspected cardiac sarcoidosis. Which preparation is most important to make the study interpretable?
options: IV beta-blocker to slow the heart rate
Oral potassium perchlorate to block thyroid uptake
Full bladder protocol with oral contrast
High-carbohydrate loading in the hour before injection
Prolonged high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet followed by a fast, sometimes with IV heparin
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Prolonged high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet followed by a fast, sometimes with IV heparin
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: This regimen switches myocardial metabolism from glucose to free fatty acids, suppressing physiological FDG uptake. Pathological inflammatory uptake then stands out against a silenced background, making the study diagnostic.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: On a well-suppressed cardiac FDG-PET combined with rest perfusion imaging, which finding best indicates active cardiac sarcoidosis amenable to immunosuppression?
options: A region of reduced perfusion with increased FDG uptake (mismatch)
Normal perfusion with no myocardial FDG uptake
Increased FDG uptake confined to the blood pool
Uniform diffuse FDG uptake throughout the entire myocardium
Matched reduction in both perfusion and FDG uptake
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A region of reduced perfusion with increased FDG uptake (mismatch)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A perfusion–metabolism mismatch reflects active granulomatous inflammation that is potentially reversible with treatment. A matched perfusion–FDG defect instead indicates established scar, and absent uptake indicates no active disease.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with a prosthetic aortic valve has persistent bacteraemia but an equivocal echocardiogram. FDG-PET/CT shows abnormal uptake around the valve sewing ring. How is this best interpreted?
options: It excludes infection and confirms a mechanical valve leak
It reliably indicates infection even one week after valve surgery
It is a major criterion for prosthetic-valve endocarditis in the ESC-modified Duke criteria
It is a normal finding for any prosthetic valve regardless of timing
It is diagnostic only of extracardiac malignancy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It is a major criterion for prosthetic-valve endocarditis in the ESC-modified Duke criteria
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Abnormal FDG uptake around a prosthetic valve is incorporated as a major criterion for prosthetic-valve endocarditis. Interpretation must account for post-operative inflammation, which causes uptake for weeks to months after surgery.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 68-year-old man has a rising PSA of 0.4 ng/mL two years after radical prostatectomy. CT abdomen/pelvis and a bone scan are both normal. Which imaging test is most likely to localise recurrent disease?
options: Transrectal ultrasound of the prostate bed
Repeat CT with contrast in 6 months
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: PSMA PET/CT
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: PSMA PET/CT detects recurrent prostate cancer at low PSA levels where CT and bone scan are typically negative. Its high tumour-to-background contrast localises small nodal and bone deposits, directing salvage therapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which of the following is a recognised cause of a false-negative PSMA PET scan in a patient with active prostate cancer?
options: A dedifferentiated neuroendocrine tumour with low PSMA expression
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A dedifferentiated neuroendocrine tumour with low PSMA expression
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Dedifferentiated and neuroendocrine prostate tumours may express little or no PSMA, so they can fail to accumulate tracer despite active disease. This is why a negative scan does not exclude cancer and must be read alongside PSA kinetics.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which structure represents normal physiological uptake on PSMA PET rather than metastatic disease?
options: A focal deposit in the L3 vertebral body
A soft-tissue nodule in the prostate bed
An enlarged avid external iliac lymph node
An avid rib lesion at a non-fracture site
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: The salivary glands
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The salivary and lacrimal glands normally show intense physiological PSMA uptake and should not be mistaken for disease. Recognising this pattern, along with renal and bowel activity, is essential for accurate reporting.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 58-year-old with biopsy-proven metastatic well-differentiated ileal NET is referred for ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT. He receives monthly long-acting lanreotide, with his last dose 5 days ago. What is the most appropriate advice regarding timing?
options: Proceed immediately; depot analogues do not affect the scan
Switch the study to an FDG-PET instead
Delay the scan and perform it just before the next depot dose is due
Give an extra subcutaneous octreotide dose on the morning of the scan
Stop all analgesia and fast for 12 hours before imaging
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Delay the scan and perform it just before the next depot dose is due
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Somatostatin analogues compete with the tracer for SSTR2 and can produce false-negative studies. Scanning at the trough, just before the next depot injection, minimises receptor blockade and maximises tumour uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which structure demonstrates physiological ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE uptake that is a well-recognised cause of a false-positive for a pancreatic NET?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Uncinate process of the pancreas
