investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The uncinate process normally accumulates tracer and is a classic pseudolesion mimicking a pancreatic NET. Correlation with the CT component and lesion morphology distinguishes physiology from a true tumour.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with a known NET has a lesion that is intensely FDG-avid but shows no uptake on ⁶⁸Ga-DOTATATE PET-CT. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: A poorly-differentiated, high-grade lesion with loss of somatostatin receptors
A well-differentiated, low-grade tumour ideal for PRRT
A technical artefact from renal tracer excretion
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A poorly-differentiated, high-grade lesion with loss of somatostatin receptors
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: As NETs dedifferentiate they lose SSTR expression and gain glucose metabolism, becoming FDG-avid but DOTATATE-negative. Such high-grade lesions carry a worse prognosis and are unsuitable for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A whole-body ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP bone scan shows diffuse, intense uptake throughout the axial skeleton with virtually no visible kidney or bladder activity. What does this pattern represent?
options: Technical failure of the gamma camera
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Superscan from widespread osteoblastic metastases
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A superscan shows avid, uniform skeletal uptake so that almost all injected tracer is bound to bone, leaving the kidneys and bladder faint or 'absent'. It reflects diffuse osteoblastic metastatic disease (or metabolic bone disease) and is a classic exam sign.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with right-upper-quadrant pain has a HIDA scan. At 60 minutes there is good hepatic uptake and tracer in the duodenum, but the gallbladder is not visualised. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute cholecystitis from cystic duct obstruction
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Acute cholecystitis from cystic duct obstruction
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Non-filling of the gallbladder at 60 minutes despite tracer reaching the bowel indicates cystic duct obstruction, the hallmark of acute cholecystitis. Passage into the duodenum confirms the common bile duct is patent, localising the block to the cystic duct.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which statement about radiation safety for a ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP bone scan is correct?
options: It delivers a higher dose than whole-body PET/CT
Iodinated contrast nephrotoxicity is the main concern
Breastfeeding can continue without any interruption
Patients should drink fluids and void frequently afterwards to reduce bladder dose
Thyroid blockade with potassium iodide is mandatory beforehand
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Patients should drink fluids and void frequently afterwards to reduce bladder dose
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: MDP is renally excreted, so hydration and frequent voiding clear tracer from the bladder and lower the gonadal and bladder radiation dose. ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP needs no thyroid blockade and involves no iodinated contrast.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 74-year-old man with HFpEF and unexplained LV wall thickening has a ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DPD scan showing myocardial uptake equal to rib uptake (Perugini grade 2). His serum free light chains, serum immunofixation and urine immunofixation are all normal. What is the most appropriate diagnostic conclusion?
options: Proceed to endomyocardial biopsy to confirm the diagnosis
The scan is negative; amyloidosis is excluded
Diagnose ATTR cardiac amyloidosis without endomyocardial biopsy
Diagnose AL cardiac amyloidosis and start chemotherapy
Repeat the scan in 12 months before deciding
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Diagnose ATTR cardiac amyloidosis without endomyocardial biopsy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A Perugini grade 2–3 scan combined with a negative monoclonal protein screen is over 99% specific for ATTR. This validated non-biopsy pathway allows a confident diagnosis without endomyocardial biopsy. Genotyping then separates hereditary from wild-type ATTR.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Why is a serum free light chain assay with serum and urine immunofixation mandatory alongside a positive bone scan?
options: To calculate the correct radiation dose for the study
To assess renal function before tracer administration
To determine whether SPECT rather than planar imaging is needed
To exclude AL amyloidosis, which can also show tracer uptake and requires urgent haematology treatment
To confirm the tracer was injected intravenously rather than subcutaneously
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: To exclude AL amyloidosis, which can also show tracer uptake and requires urgent haematology treatment
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: AL amyloid occasionally produces myocardial tracer uptake, so a positive scan is not specific on its own. A negative monoclonal screen rules out AL, which is a haematological emergency needing prompt treatment. Only then can the scan be attributed to ATTR.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which finding on a bone-avid tracer study is regarded as POSITIVE for cardiac ATTR amyloidosis?
options: Tracer confined to the blood pool on early imaging
Grade 1 uptake, less than bone, on planar imaging only
A heart:contralateral ratio of 0.8 at one hour
Perugini grade 0 with normal skeletal uptake
Perugini grade 2–3 myocardial uptake (cardiac uptake equal to or greater than bone)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Perugini grade 2–3 myocardial uptake (cardiac uptake equal to or greater than bone)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Grade 2 (cardiac equal to bone) and grade 3 (cardiac greater than bone with reduced skeletal signal) are the positive categories. A supportive heart:contralateral ratio is 1.5 or higher at one hour. SPECT confirms the uptake is truly myocardial.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A diabetic patient has focal increased uptake on the flow, blood-pool AND delayed images of a three-phase bone scan of the foot. What does this pattern most support?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Osteomyelitis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Positivity in all three phases indicates increased blood flow, soft-tissue hyperaemia and, critically, osteoblastic bone uptake. This triad is the classic scintigraphic pattern of osteomyelitis.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: In three-phase bone scintigraphy, which phase best distinguishes osteomyelitis from cellulitis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: The delayed (2–4h) bone phase
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Cellulitis increases the flow and blood-pool phases but shows no focal delayed uptake because bone is not involved. Focal uptake on the delayed bone phase indicates true osteoblastic bone infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which agent is used to improve specificity for infection when a three-phase bone scan is positive near recent surgery or metalwork?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled white cells (HMPAO leucocytes)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Labelled white-cell scanning (⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO or ¹¹¹In-oxine leucocytes) accumulates at sites of active infection rather than bland bone remodelling. It is the standard adjunct where bone turnover is already raised by surgery, fracture or hardware.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with a dilated left pelvicalyceal system undergoes a MAG3 renogram. The left curve rises steadily and does not fall; after IV frusemide there is still no washout. What does this indicate?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: True mechanical obstruction
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A curve that keeps rising and fails to wash out after a diuretic challenge is the hallmark of genuine obstruction. The diuretic forces a high urine flow, so a truly obstructed system cannot drain and retains tracer.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Why is ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAG3 generally preferred over ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DTPA for dynamic renography?
options: It is the only agent measuring split function
It is filtered rather than secreted
It is tubularly secreted with high extraction, giving better images in poor function
It contains iodine for better contrast
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It is tubularly secreted with high extraction, giving better images in poor function
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: MAG3 is actively secreted by the proximal tubules and has a high extraction fraction, producing superior image quality. This advantage is greatest in kidneys with impaired function, where DTPA's filtered images are poor.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which additional agent is administered during renography to investigate renovascular hypertension from renal artery stenosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Captopril
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Captopril is an ACE inhibitor that removes efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, unmasking a functionally significant renal artery stenosis. The stenosed kidney's renogram curve deteriorates after captopril compared with baseline.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which cellular process explains the renal localisation of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA?
options: Uptake by medullary loops of Henle
Binding and retention within proximal tubular cells of the cortex
Active secretion into the collecting ducts
Glomerular filtration with rapid tubular excretion
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Binding and retention within proximal tubular cells of the cortex
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: DMSA is bound and fixed in proximal tubular cells, so it accumulates in and marks functioning cortex. This cortical retention with minimal excretion is what makes it ideal for scar detection and split function.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A child has a DMSA scan showing a focal cold cortical defect with a preserved renal outline and no volume loss. What is the most likely interpretation?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Acute pyelonephritis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Acute pyelonephritis produces photopenic defects while the renal outline and volume are preserved. A scar, by contrast, shows volume loss and cortical thinning.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: When is imaging typically performed after intravenous injection of ⁹⁹ᵐTc-DMSA?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: At 2–4 hours
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Imaging at 2–4 hours allows cortical fixation of the tracer and clearance of background activity. This delay gives the clean static cortical images DMSA is valued for.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 40-year-old woman with a suppressed TSH and raised free T4 has thyroid scintigraphy showing diffuse, homogeneously increased uptake throughout an enlarged gland. What is the most likely diagnosis?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Graves' disease
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Diffuse, homogeneously increased uptake across the whole enlarged gland is the classic scintigraphic pattern of Graves' disease. The autoantibody-driven stimulation activates the entire gland uniformly.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient booked for ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate thyroid scintigraphy had a contrast-enhanced CT with iodinated contrast three days ago. Why should the scan be deferred?
options: The contrast increases the radiation dose to unsafe levels
Iodinated contrast reacts chemically with technetium
Iodinated contrast triggers a hypersensitivity reaction to the tracer
Contrast causes the thyroid to organify pertechnetate
The iodine load saturates the sodium-iodide symporter and blunts tracer uptake
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: The iodine load saturates the sodium-iodide symporter and blunts tracer uptake
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Recent iodinated contrast delivers a large iodine load that competes at the sodium-iodide symporter, producing falsely low uptake and an uninterpretable scan. Imaging is deferred until the iodine load clears.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Thyroid scintigraphy of a solitary palpable nodule shows the nodule as an area of absent tracer uptake (a 'cold' nodule). What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and discharge as this indicates a benign adenoma
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A cold nodule is hypofunctioning and carries a slightly increased risk of malignancy compared with a hot nodule. It warrants fine-needle aspiration cytology to characterise it.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 34-year-old woman with thyrotoxicosis undergoes a radioactive iodine uptake scan, which shows markedly reduced, near-absent uptake throughout the gland. Which diagnosis does this pattern best support?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Thyroiditis causes thyrotoxicosis from release of preformed hormone by damaged follicles, so trapping of new iodine falls and uptake is low. Graves' and toxic nodular disease both drive active hormone synthesis and therefore show high uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which statement about ¹³¹I radioiodine therapy is correct?
options: It is safe to administer during the first trimester of pregnancy
It is the treatment of choice for thyrotoxicosis due to thyroiditis
Breastfeeding may continue normally during treatment
A low-iodine diet reduces its effectiveness and should be avoided
Its beta emission delivers a local ablative dose to functioning thyroid tissue
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Its beta emission delivers a local ablative dose to functioning thyroid tissue
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: ¹³¹I emits beta particles that are concentrated by functioning cells and destroy them locally, making it effective for Graves', toxic nodules and thyroid cancer. Pregnancy and breastfeeding are absolute contraindications, and thyroiditis has low uptake so radioiodine is ineffective.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A woman is scheduled for ¹³¹I ablation after total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Which pre-treatment step maximises iodine uptake by residual thyroid tissue?
options: Administering iodinated CT contrast the day before
A low-iodine diet with stimulation by thyroid hormone withdrawal or rhTSH
Starting a high-iodine diet with kelp supplements
Giving a saturated solution of potassium iodide beforehand
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A low-iodine diet with stimulation by thyroid hormone withdrawal or rhTSH
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Depleting the body iodine pool with a low-iodine diet increases avidity for the radioiodine, and raising TSH by hormone withdrawal or recombinant TSH (rhTSH) stimulates NIS-mediated uptake. Iodine loads such as contrast, kelp, amiodarone or potassium iodide saturate the gland and block uptake.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A thyroid nodule FNA is reported as Thy3f (follicular neoplasm). What is the most appropriate management?
options: Repeat the fine-needle aspiration in 6 months
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Diagnostic hemithyroidectomy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Thy3f indicates a follicular neoplasm, but cytology cannot distinguish a benign adenoma from a carcinoma because that requires assessment of capsular/vascular invasion. Diagnostic hemithyroidectomy provides the capsule histology needed to make that distinction.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A thyroid nodule FNA yields an inadequate sample reported as Thy1. What is the correct next step?
options: Reassure the patient that the nodule is benign
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Repeat the ultrasound-guided FNA
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Thy1 means the aspirate was non-diagnostic or inadequate and yields no information about malignancy risk. The appropriate action is to repeat the FNA under ultrasound guidance, targeting any solid component to improve cellular yield.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which feature on thyroid ultrasound most strongly suggests malignancy and would prompt FNA?
options: Punctate microcalcification with a taller-than-wide shape
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Punctate microcalcification with a taller-than-wide shape
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Punctate microcalcification and a taller-than-wide (anteroposterior greater than transverse) shape are classic U4/U5 sonographic features of malignancy, particularly papillary carcinoma. These indeterminate-to-suspicious features are the ones that select a nodule for FNA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which property must an isotope GFR tracer such as ⁵¹Cr-EDTA possess for its plasma clearance to equal the GFR?
options: It is highly protein-bound in plasma
It is actively secreted by the proximal tubule
It is freely filtered but not secreted or reabsorbed by the tubules
It is metabolised by the renal parenchyma
It is partially reabsorbed in the distal tubule
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It is freely filtered but not secreted or reabsorbed by the tubules
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A valid GFR marker crosses the glomerular filter freely and is neither secreted nor reabsorbed, so filtration is its only route of clearance. This makes its plasma clearance a direct measure of glomerular filtration rate.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 62-year-old woman needs carboplatin chemotherapy dosed by the Calvert formula. Why is an isotope GFR requested rather than relying on creatinine-based eGFR?
options: It provides an accurate measured GFR needed for safe carboplatin dosing
It avoids any radiation exposure to the patient
It measures renal blood flow rather than filtration
It is quicker and needs no blood sampling
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It provides an accurate measured GFR needed for safe carboplatin dosing
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Carboplatin is dosed by the Calvert formula, dose = AUC × (GFR + 25), so an inaccurate GFR risks toxicity or underdosing. Isotope GFR directly measures filtration and is the reference standard when precision matters.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During an isotope GFR study, which factor most threatens the accuracy of the calculated result?
options: Use of the opposite arm for venous sampling
The patient having a normal serum creatinine
Reporting the result corrected to body surface area
A low background radiation dose from the tracer
Marked extracellular fluid overload with ascites and oedema
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Marked extracellular fluid overload with ascites and oedema
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: In gross ECF expansion the tracer distributes into the enlarged fluid compartment and equilibrates slowly, distorting the clearance curve. Extended or multi-sample protocols are needed to obtain a reliable value in these patients.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 27-year-old pregnant woman has suspected PE and a normal chest X-ray. Which V/Q finding would most strongly indicate pulmonary embolism?
options: Increased perfusion to the upper zones
A normal perfusion scan with a small ventilation defect
Matched ventilation and perfusion defects in the right base
Uniformly reduced ventilation across both lungs
A segmental perfusion defect with preserved ventilation in the same region
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A segmental perfusion defect with preserved ventilation in the same region
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: PE occludes a pulmonary artery, abolishing perfusion while ventilation to that segment remains intact. This perfusion–ventilation mismatch is the diagnostic hallmark of pulmonary embolism.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which radiopharmaceutical is injected intravenously for the perfusion component of a V/Q scan, and how does it localise?
options: ¹²³I that concentrates in thyroid tissue
¹⁸F-FDG taken up by metabolically active cells
⁸¹ᵐKr gas that fills the alveoli
⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA particles that lodge in pulmonary capillaries
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MAA particles that lodge in pulmonary capillaries
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Macroaggregated albumin particles are large enough to microembolise and lodge in the pulmonary capillary bed after IV injection, mapping regional blood flow. Only a tiny fraction of capillaries is occluded, so the study is safe.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: In which patient is a V/Q scan the most appropriate first-line investigation for suspected PE?
options: A patient with extensive bilateral pulmonary oedema on CXR
A patient with a known allergy to macroaggregated albumin
A patient with a large right-to-left cardiac shunt
A young woman with a normal chest X-ray and a documented severe iodinated contrast allergy
A patient whose chest X-ray shows dense right lower lobe consolidation
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A young woman with a normal chest X-ray and a documented severe iodinated contrast allergy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A V/Q scan avoids iodinated contrast and spares breast radiation, making it ideal when CTPA is contraindicated. A normal chest X-ray maximises specificity, giving the most interpretable result.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient undergoes SPECT MPI. The inferior wall shows reduced tracer uptake on the stress images but normal uptake on the rest images. What does this pattern indicate?
options: Inducible ischaemia in the inferior (RCA) territory
Full-thickness infarct of the inferior wall
A normal study with no significant coronary disease
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Inducible ischaemia in the inferior (RCA) territory
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A defect that is abnormal on stress but normalises at rest is a reversible defect, the signature of inducible ischaemia from a flow-limiting stenosis. The inferior wall corresponds to the right coronary artery territory. The myocardium is viable, which is why perfusion recovers at rest.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which instruction is essential before pharmacological stress MPI using adenosine?
options: Fast the patient for 6 hours to reduce bowel tracer uptake
Withhold caffeine and theophylline for at least 12–24 hours beforehand
Give prophylactic salbutamol nebuliser to all patients
Load with a beta-blocker on the morning of the test
Administer thyroid blockade with potassium iodide the day before
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Withhold caffeine and theophylline for at least 12–24 hours beforehand
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Caffeine and theophylline are competitive adenosine-receptor antagonists that blunt the vasodilator response and cause false-negative studies. They must be stopped for around 12–24 hours before adenosine or dipyridamole stress. This preparation preserves the sensitivity of the test for detecting ischaemia.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with brittle asthma needs a functional test for suspected coronary disease and cannot exercise. Which stress method is most appropriate?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Dobutamine stress
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Adenosine, dipyridamole and regadenoson are vasodilators that can precipitate bronchospasm and are contraindicated in significant asthma. Dobutamine works by increasing myocardial oxygen demand through inotropy and chronotropy, avoiding adenosine-receptor stimulation. It is the preferred pharmacological stressor when the patient cannot exercise and vasodilators are unsafe.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with biochemically confirmed phaeochromocytoma is booked for a 123I-MIBG scan. Which preparation is essential to protect a specific organ from the radiopharmaceutical?
options: Oral bicarbonate loading to protect the bladder
Corticosteroid premedication to protect the adrenal cortex
Intravenous N-acetylcysteine to protect the kidneys
Potassium iodide (thyroid blockade) before and after the scan
Prophylactic amiodarone to protect the myocardium
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Potassium iodide (thyroid blockade) before and after the scan
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: MIBG is labelled with radioiodine, and free radioiodine is concentrated by the thyroid. Potassium iodide or Lugol's iodine saturates the thyroid so it cannot take up the radioiodine, shielding it from radiation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: An MIBG scan for suspected phaeochromocytoma is reported as negative despite convincing biochemistry. Which of the patient's medications is the most likely cause of a false-negative result?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Labetalol
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Labetalol is a combined alpha/beta blocker that interferes with MIBG uptake and storage at the noradrenaline transporter. Failing to withhold it can produce a false-negative scan, so it must be stopped for an appropriate washout period.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which finding on a 24-hour MIBG scan represents normal physiological uptake rather than tumour?
options: A rim of uptake around a liver metastasis
Intense focal uptake in an enlarged extra-adrenal soft-tissue mass
Multiple foci of uptake throughout the axial skeleton
A discrete focus of uptake in a lumbar vertebral body
Activity in the salivary glands, myocardium, liver and bladder
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Activity in the salivary glands, myocardium, liver and bladder
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Salivary glands, myocardium, liver, spleen, bowel and the urinary tract show expected physiological MIBG uptake. Uptake in bone, discrete masses or nodal deposits outside these sites indicates tumour.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A DaTscan (¹²³I-ioflupane SPECT) primarily images the integrity of which structure?
options: Amyloid plaque burden in the cortex
Cerebral blood flow in the basal ganglia
The presynaptic dopamine transporter on nigrostriatal terminals
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: The presynaptic dopamine transporter on nigrostriatal terminals
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Ioflupane is a cocaine analogue that binds the presynaptic dopamine transporter (DAT) on dopaminergic terminals in the striatum. Loss of tracer signal reflects loss of these presynaptic terminals, marking a true nigrostriatal degeneration.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 62-year-old has an asymmetric tremor and rigidity. A DaTscan shows reduced striatal uptake with loss of the putaminal tail. What does this reliably indicate?
options: Parkinson's disease specifically, excluding MSA and PSP
A presynaptic dopaminergic deficit consistent with a degenerative parkinsonian syndrome
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A presynaptic dopaminergic deficit consistent with a degenerative parkinsonian syndrome
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Reduced, asymmetric striatal uptake confirms a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit. This pattern is shared by Parkinson's disease, MSA and PSP, so it establishes degeneration without identifying the specific syndrome.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which preparation step is specifically required before administering ¹²³I-ioflupane?
options: Bowel preparation with an osmotic laxative
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Thyroid blockade with potassium iodide
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Free radioiodide (¹²³I⁻) released from the tracer concentrates in the thyroid, so potassium iodide is given to saturate and protect the gland. Drugs affecting DAT binding are also withheld, but thyroid blockade is the isotope-specific requirement.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 68-year-old with recurrent obscure PR bleeding has negative OGD and colonoscopy. Labelled RBC scintigraphy is requested. Which radiopharmaceutical is used?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled autologous red blood cells
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Labelled RBC scintigraphy tags the patient's own red cells with ⁹⁹ᵐTc so they remain in the vascular pool. A leak into the bowel lumen then shows as an abnormal focus of extravasated activity.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: On a dynamic labelled RBC study, which finding confirms active gastrointestinal bleeding?
options: A fixed focus over the cardiac blood pool
Diffuse activity in the urinary bladder
A focus of activity that appears and migrates along the bowel with peristalsis
Persistent uniform blood-pool activity in the great vessels
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A focus of activity that appears and migrates along the bowel with peristalsis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: True luminal bleeding produces a focus that increases in intensity and moves along the bowel over sequential frames. Fixed vascular or excreted activity is expected normal biodistribution.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 3-year-old boy presents with painless rectal bleeding. Which scan and tracer best identifies the likely cause?
options: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled RBC scan for slow venous ooze
⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate Meckel's scan detecting ectopic gastric mucosa
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate Meckel's scan detecting ectopic gastric mucosa
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Painless PR bleeding in a young child suggests a Meckel's diverticulum containing ectopic gastric mucosa. Free ⁹⁹ᵐTc-pertechnetate is concentrated by that mucosa, producing a focus in the right lower quadrant.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with a painful hip prosthesis and raised inflammatory markers has an equivocal MRI degraded by metal artefact. Which combination best confirms or excludes prosthetic joint infection?
options: Labelled white cell scan combined with a ⁹⁹ᵐTc bone marrow scan
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Labelled white cell scan combined with a ⁹⁹ᵐTc bone marrow scan
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Labelled leucocytes accumulate at sites of active infection, and the marrow scan distinguishes true infection from physiological marrow uptake. Infection is shown by white-cell uptake that is not matched on the marrow map, which maximises specificity around a prosthesis.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: On serial imaging, which finding on a labelled white cell scan most strongly indicates active infection?
options: A focus that fades in intensity on delayed images
Intense uptake confined to the spleen
Diffuse blood-pool activity that clears uniformly
Uptake in liver and bone marrow only
A focus of uptake that increases in intensity and extent between early and delayed images
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A focus of uptake that increases in intensity and extent between early and delayed images
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Ongoing recruitment of labelled neutrophils to an infective focus causes uptake to rise over time. Physiological splenic, hepatic and marrow activity form the expected normal distribution, and a fading focus argues against infection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which radiopharmaceutical is preferred for a labelled white cell scan investigating a suspected intra-abdominal collection because it shows no physiological bowel excretion?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ¹¹¹In-oxine labelled leucocytes
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: ¹¹¹In-oxine provides a very stable intracellular label with no bowel or urinary excretion, so abdominal foci are not obscured by physiological gut activity. ⁹⁹ᵐTc-HMPAO shows delayed bowel, urinary and gallbladder clearance that can confound abdominal interpretation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A woman with early invasive breast cancer and a clinically node-negative axilla undergoes sentinel lymph node biopsy. What is the principal benefit of this approach compared with routine axillary clearance?
options: It avoids the morbidity of full axillary dissection, chiefly lymphoedema, when the node is negative
It removes the need for any histological examination of nodes
It guarantees no further surgery will ever be required
It delivers a higher radiation dose to sterilise tumour cells
It replaces the need for adjuvant systemic therapy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: It avoids the morbidity of full axillary dissection, chiefly lymphoedema, when the node is negative
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A negative sentinel node reliably predicts a tumour-free basin, so completion axillary dissection can be safely omitted. This spares the patient the lymphoedema, nerve injury and shoulder morbidity of full clearance, which is the central rationale for SLNB.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which agent is injected around the tumour to localise the sentinel node on lymphoscintigraphy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-labelled nanocolloid
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: ⁹⁹ᵐTc-nanocolloid particles are small enough to enter lymphatics and are trapped in the first draining node, marking it as a focal hot spot. The node is then found with a gamma probe at surgery, often alongside blue dye.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During a sentinel node biopsy the patient becomes hypotensive with a fall in measured oxygen saturation shortly after the intra-operative dye is given. Which agent is the most likely cause?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Patent blue dye
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Patent blue dye carries a recognised risk of anaphylaxis, presenting with hypotension and cardiovascular collapse. It also causes an artefactual drop in pulse-oximetry readings, so the anaesthetist should be forewarned before it is injected.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: An MIBG scan confirms a phaeochromocytoma. In preparing the patient for surgery, which is essential?
options: Alpha-blockade must be established before any beta-blockade
No blockade is needed before surgery
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Alpha-blockade must be established before any beta-blockade
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Phaeochromocytoma is resected surgically, but pharmacological preparation is essential: alpha-blockade (e.g. phenoxybenzamine) FIRST to control blood pressure, then beta-blockade. Beta-blockade before alpha-blockade leaves alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed and can precipitate a hypertensive crisis.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 68-year-old with disabling calf claudication despite exercise and statin therapy has a focal 2 cm superficial femoral artery stenosis. Which access is most appropriate for treating this ipsilateral femoropopliteal lesion?
options: Retrograde contralateral common femoral puncture with up-and-over technique only
Direct popliteal artery puncture as first choice
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Antegrade common femoral artery puncture
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Antegrade puncture of the ipsilateral common femoral artery gives the most direct pushability and support for femoropopliteal and infrapopliteal work. It is the standard route for treating lesions distal to the puncture in the same limb.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During balloon angioplasty of an iliac stenosis the patient develops sudden severe back pain, hypotension, and the completion run shows contrast extravasation. What is the immediate management?
options: Administer a bolus of intravenous heparin
Remove all wires and catheters immediately and reverse the patient
Reinflate a balloon across the site to tamponade and prepare a covered stent
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Reinflate a balloon across the site to tamponade and prepare a covered stent
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Vessel rupture is a life-threatening complication managed by keeping wire access, inflating a balloon to tamponade the bleeding, and deploying a covered stent. Maintaining wire position across the site is essential so definitive treatment can be delivered rapidly.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which pre-procedure measure most directly reduces the risk of contrast-induced nephropathy before peripheral angioplasty?
options: Adequate hydration and minimising iodinated contrast volume
Loading with high-dose aspirin and clopidogrel
Withholding all antiplatelet agents for a week
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Adequate hydration and minimising iodinated contrast volume
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Contrast nephropathy risk is lowered chiefly by peri-procedural hydration and using the smallest effective volume of iodinated contrast, especially in renal impairment. Renal function is checked beforehand to identify at-risk patients.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with massive lower GI bleeding undergoes catheter angiography. Which single finding on DSA confirms active haemorrhage and identifies the target for embolisation?
options: A smoothly tapering artery with no filling defect
Symmetrical arterial narrowing throughout the mesenteric circulation
Focal contrast extravasation from a branch vessel persisting into the venous phase
Uniform mucosal blush of the entire colon
Delayed venous drainage of the whole territory
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Focal contrast extravasation from a branch vessel persisting into the venous phase
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Active bleeding is seen as focal contrast that leaves the vessel lumen and pools, persisting after the arterial phase. This localises the culprit vessel so the microcatheter can be advanced for superselective embolisation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which embolic agent is specifically chosen because it is temporary and allows the vessel to recanalise, making it favoured in trauma and post-partum haemorrhage?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Gelfoam (gelatin sponge)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Gelfoam is a resorbable gelatin sponge that occludes the vessel for days and then recanalises, allowing the tissue to recover once bleeding has stopped. This makes it well suited to preserving organ viability in trauma and uterine embolisation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Bronchial artery embolisation for massive haemoptysis carries a specific serious risk that mandates careful catheter positioning. What is it?
options: Post-embolisation syndrome causing permanent lung fibrosis
Spinal cord ischaemia from non-target embolisation of a spinal artery
Systemic air embolism from the embolic particles
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Spinal cord ischaemia from non-target embolisation of a spinal artery
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The anterior spinal artery can arise from or share supply with bronchial arteries, so reflux of embolic material can infarct the cord and cause paraplegia. Superselective catheterisation distal to any spinal branch and controlled injection are used to avoid this.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 42-year-old woman undergoes UAE for symptomatic fibroids. Three days later she has crampy pelvic pain, malaise, nausea and a temperature of 37.8°C, but no offensive discharge. What is the most likely explanation?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Post-embolisation syndrome
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Crampy pelvic pain, low-grade fever, nausea and malaise in the first days after embolisation are the classic features of expected post-embolisation syndrome. It is self-limiting and managed with analgesia, NSAIDs and antiemetics rather than antibiotics.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which angiographic finding is characteristically sought and treated during uterine artery embolisation for fibroids?
options: A saccular berry aneurysm at the circle of Willis
Hypervascular fibroid blush supplied by hypertrophied uterine arteries
Renal artery stenosis with post-stenotic dilatation
Avascular filling defect in the portal vein
String-of-beads appearance of the internal carotid artery
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Hypervascular fibroid blush supplied by hypertrophied uterine arteries
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Fibroids are hypervascular and produce a tumour "blush" fed by enlarged, tortuous uterine arteries. Embolic particles are injected to occlude this supply until the blush disappears and near-stasis is achieved bilaterally.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 34-year-old woman with symptomatic fibroids wishes to conceive in the future. Which statement should guide her counselling?
options: Fibroids never affect fertility so no intervention is needed
Hysterectomy is the recommended fertility-preserving option
UAE guarantees improved fertility by shrinking the fibroids
UAE is the definitive first-line treatment for women wanting to preserve fertility
Myomectomy is generally preferred because UAE may reduce ovarian reserve and fertility
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Myomectomy is generally preferred because UAE may reduce ovarian reserve and fertility
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: UAE carries a risk of non-target ovarian embolisation, diminished ovarian reserve and reduced fertility. For women who wish to preserve fertility, myomectomy is generally the preferred uterine-sparing option.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Transarterial chemoembolisation targets liver tumours effectively because the tumour blood supply differs from normal liver. What is the predominant blood supply of hepatocellular carcinoma?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Hepatic artery
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: HCC and hypervascular liver metastases derive their blood supply predominantly from the hepatic artery, while normal parenchyma is mainly portal-vein supplied. This differential lets arterially delivered agents concentrate in tumour and spare normal liver.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient is being worked up for Yttrium-90 radioembolisation of unresectable HCC. Which pre-treatment investigation is specifically required to assess safety before the therapeutic dose?
options: 99mTc-MAA mapping scan to measure lung shunt fraction
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: 99mTc-MAA mapping scan to measure lung shunt fraction
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: TARE requires a mapping angiogram with 99mTc-labelled macroaggregated albumin to quantify the lung shunt fraction and detect GI non-target deposition. A high shunt fraction predicts radiation pneumonitis and can reduce the deliverable dose or contraindicate treatment.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which finding would most strongly favour radioembolisation (TARE) over conventional chemoembolisation (TACE) in a patient with HCC?
options: Child-Pugh C cirrhosis with refractory ascites
A solitary 2 cm peripheral nodule amenable to ablation
An INR of 4.0 that cannot be corrected
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Main portal vein tumour thrombosis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: TARE is minimally embolic and kills by internal radiation rather than ischaemia, making it the safer choice when portal inflow is compromised by main portal vein thrombosis. TACE carries a higher risk of ischaemic hepatic decompensation in this setting.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 34-year-old woman has extensive left iliofemoral DVT and is being considered for catheter-directed thrombolysis. What is the main long-term benefit that justifies this approach in a selected younger patient?
options: Reduction in the risk of post-thrombotic syndrome
Permanent cure of an underlying thrombophilia
Elimination of the need for any anticoagulation afterwards
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Reduction in the risk of post-thrombotic syndrome
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Clearing extensive proximal iliofemoral thrombus preserves venous valve function and patency, lowering the incidence of post-thrombotic syndrome. This benefit is why CDT is offered to selected younger patients with low bleeding risk.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During a catheter-directed thrombolysis infusion, which laboratory parameter is monitored to gauge the systemic effect of the thrombolytic and guide dose adjustment?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Fibrinogen
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Fibrinogen is consumed during systemic fibrinolysis, so a falling level signals increased bleeding risk. Monitoring it allows the operator to reduce or stop the infusion before major haemorrhage occurs.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with acute limb ischaemia from a thrombosed graft is assessed for thrombolysis. Which finding is an absolute contraindication to the thrombolytic agent?
options: A remote appendicectomy ten years ago
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A recent haemorrhagic stroke
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Recent intracranial haemorrhage dramatically raises the risk of fatal bleeding with systemic fibrinolytic activity and is an absolute contraindication. Thrombolysis must be avoided and alternative revascularisation considered.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 28-year-old man is referred for embolisation of a symptomatic left varicocele. Why is the left side most commonly affected?
options: The left gonadal vein is compressed by the sigmoid colon
The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a near right angle, raising venous pressure and promoting reflux
The left testicular artery is congenitally absent
The right renal vein compresses the left gonadal vein
The left gonadal vein drains directly into the portal vein
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a near right angle, raising venous pressure and promoting reflux
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The left gonadal vein enters the left renal vein at a near right angle, creating a higher-pressure, longer venous column that predisposes to valvular incompetence and reflux. The right gonadal vein drains obliquely and directly into the IVC, so right-sided varicoceles are less common.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which venous access route is typically used for gonadal vein embolisation?
options: Great saphenous vein at the ankle
Right internal jugular or common femoral vein
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Right internal jugular or common femoral vein
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Access is gained through a large central vein, usually the right internal jugular or the common femoral vein, under ultrasound guidance. From there the catheter is advanced to the left renal vein and selectively into the gonadal vein.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness immediately after coil placement during gonadal vein embolisation. Which complication is most likely?
options: Coil migration to the pulmonary circulation
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Coil migration to the pulmonary circulation
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A dislodged coil can travel from the gonadal vein through the renal vein and IVC to the pulmonary circulation, producing acute pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. Correct coil sizing and controlled deployment reduce this risk, and migrated coils may require percutaneous retrieval.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 62-year-old man has a large proximal femoral DVT confirmed on Doppler. He is 3 days post major intracranial haemorrhage and cannot receive anticoagulation. What is the most appropriate intervention to prevent pulmonary embolism?
options: Insertion of a retrievable IVC filter
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Insertion of a retrievable IVC filter
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: This patient has proven VTE with an absolute contraindication to anticoagulation because of recent intracranial haemorrhage. A retrievable IVC filter mechanically prevents lower-limb emboli from causing PE while anticoagulation is withheld, and can be removed once anticoagulation becomes safe.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During IVC filter insertion, at what level is the device most commonly deployed?
options: In the infrarenal IVC just below the lowest renal vein
In the suprarenal IVC above both renal veins
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: In the infrarenal IVC just below the lowest renal vein
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The filter is normally positioned in the infrarenal IVC with its apex just below the lowest renal vein. This location traps emboli from the legs and pelvis while preserving renal venous drainage above the device should the filter thrombose.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which statement about retrievable IVC filters is correct?
options: They should be removed once anticoagulation can be safely resumed
They eliminate the need for any future anticoagulation
They dissolve spontaneously within a few weeks
They provide definitive treatment of the underlying DVT
They reduce the incidence of recurrent lower-limb DVT
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: They should be removed once anticoagulation can be safely resumed
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Retrievable filters are intended for temporary use and should be removed once anticoagulation can be safely started or the high-risk period has passed. Retained filters accumulate complications such as fracture, penetration and IVC occlusion, so timely retrieval is essential.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient requires intermittent chemotherapy over many months and wants the device with the lowest infection risk and best cosmetic outcome. Which is the most appropriate central venous access device?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Implantable port
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A totally implantable port is entirely subcutaneous and accessed by a needle only when needed, giving it the lowest catheter-related infection rate. Its buried reservoir also offers the best cosmesis, making it ideal for intermittent long-term chemotherapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Immediately after ultrasound- and fluoroscopy-guided insertion of a right internal jugular tunnelled line, what investigation is mandatory before the catheter is used?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Chest radiograph
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A post-procedure chest radiograph confirms the catheter tip lies at the cavoatrial junction and excludes a pneumothorax. This must be checked before the line is used for infusions.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which measure most directly reduces the risk of arterial puncture and pneumothorax during central venous access?
options: Placing the patient head-up during puncture
Real-time ultrasound guidance of the venous puncture
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Real-time ultrasound guidance of the venous puncture
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Real-time ultrasound lets the operator visualise the vein, adjacent artery and pleura and direct the needle precisely into the vein. This directly lowers rates of inadvertent arterial puncture and pneumothorax compared with landmark technique.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 62-year-old man has a rim-enhancing 7 cm pelvic collection following a perforated diverticulum. What is the most appropriate first-line management for this accessible, infected collection?
options: Oral antibiotics alone with outpatient review
Watchful waiting with repeat CT in 6 weeks
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Image-guided percutaneous catheter drainage
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Percutaneous drainage under US or CT guidance is first-line for an accessible infected collection, achieving source control while avoiding the morbidity of open surgery. It also provides a sample for microbiology to guide antibiotic therapy.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During Seldinger insertion of a drainage catheter, what step immediately follows passing the guidewire into the collection?
options: Direct trocar advancement alongside the wire
Connection of the wire to suction drainage
Serial dilatation of the tract over the wire
Removal of the guidewire before any dilatation
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Serial dilatation of the tract over the wire
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: In the Seldinger technique the tract is serially dilated over the guidewire to accommodate the catheter. The locking pigtail catheter is then railroaded over the wire into the collection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with a multiloculated empyema is draining poorly through a well-positioned chest drain. Which intervention best improves drainage?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Intrapleural tPA plus DNase
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Instilled intrapleural tPA breaks down fibrinous septations while DNase reduces the viscosity of the fluid, together improving drainage of a loculated empyema. This medical adjunct frequently avoids the need for surgical decortication.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 68-year-old woman with known cervical cancer presents with fever, rigors, loin pain and a raised creatinine. CT shows a right hydronephrosis with an obstructing pelvic mass, and urine dip is positive. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Elective retrograde ureteric stent in two weeks
Oral antibiotics and outpatient urology review
Urgent percutaneous nephrostomy to decompress the system
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Urgent percutaneous nephrostomy to decompress the system
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: This is an infected obstructed kidney (pyonephrosis), a urological emergency. Urgent decompression by nephrostomy drains the pus and relieves obstruction, which is life-saving alongside intravenous antibiotics and resuscitation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During percutaneous nephrostomy, which calyx is the preferred target for the initial puncture?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: A posterior lower-pole calyx
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: A posterior calyx lies in the relatively avascular plane of the kidney, reducing the risk of major haemorrhage. A lower-pole approach stays below the pleural reflection, minimising the risk of pneumothorax.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which complication is most directly related to the highly vascular nature of the kidney following percutaneous nephrostomy?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Renal arteriovenous fistula or pseudoaneurysm
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The kidney is a highly vascular organ, so tract creation can injure vessels and produce an arteriovenous fistula or pseudoaneurysm. Significant or persistent bleeding may require angiographic embolisation to control it.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 68-year-old man with a hilar cholangiocarcinoma and obstructive jaundice needs biliary decompression. ERCP failed because the tumour prevented the wire crossing the hilum. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat identical ERCP the following day
CT-guided liver biopsy of the tumour
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Percutaneous transhepatic biliary drainage
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: High hilar strictures that defeat ERCP are the classic indication for the percutaneous transhepatic route. It allows contrast opacification of the ducts, wire passage across the block, and placement of a drain or stent to relieve the jaundice.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which pre-procedure abnormality most directly increases bleeding risk in a jaundiced patient undergoing PTC and requires correction beforehand?
options: Prolonged INR from vitamin K deficiency
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Prolonged INR from vitamin K deficiency
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Biliary obstruction impairs absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K, prolonging the INR and predisposing to bleeding along the transhepatic tract. It is corrected with IV vitamin K and, if needed, fresh frozen plasma before the procedure.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Two hours after PTBD a patient develops rigors, fever and hypotension. Which complication does this best represent?
options: Delayed allergic rash to local anaesthetic
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Cholangitis and biliary sepsis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Instrumentation and contrast injection into an infected, obstructed biliary system release bacteria into the circulation, producing rigors, fever and hypotension. Prompt antibiotics and ensuring adequate drainage are the priorities.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with an obstructing oesophageal tumour needs long-term feeding, but an endoscope cannot be passed. Which gastrostomy technique is most appropriate?
options: Open surgical gastrostomy as first line
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Radiologically-inserted gastrostomy (RIG)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: RIG uses fluoroscopy and NG-tube insufflation of the stomach, so it does not require an endoscope to pass the obstructing tumour. It is the standard choice when a per-oral endoscopic PEG is impossible.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During a RIG, what is the purpose of placing T-fasteners (gastropexy)?
options: To provide the radiopharmaceutical tracer for imaging
To dilate the oesophagus before tube passage
To measure gastric pH before feeding
To anchor the stomach to the abdominal wall and reduce leak/peritonitis
To block the pylorus and prevent reflux
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: To anchor the stomach to the abdominal wall and reduce leak/peritonitis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Gastropexy uses T-fasteners to oppose the gastric wall against the anterior abdominal wall. This secures the tract and lowers the risk of intraperitoneal leakage and peritonitis after tube placement.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient develops new severe abdominal pain, fever and tachycardia hours after a RIG. What is the most likely serious complication?
options: Peritonitis from tube misplacement or intraperitoneal leak
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Peritonitis from tube misplacement or intraperitoneal leak
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Peritonism with fever and tachycardia after gastrostomy points to the tube lying outside the stomach or leakage of gastric contents into the peritoneum. Management is to stop the feed, perform a contrast tube-check, and escalate urgently.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 58-year-old with a chest port presents with a fractured catheter fragment that has embolised to the right atrium on chest radiograph. Which device is the first-line tool for percutaneous retrieval?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Loop (gooseneck) snare
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The loop snare is the workhorse device for intravascular foreign body retrieval. It is passed over a free end of the fragment, tightened to grip it, and the fragment is withdrawn through a sheath. Forceps and baskets serve as adjuncts when no free end is available.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During snare retrieval of an embolised catheter fragment from the right heart, the patient suddenly becomes hypotensive and tachycardic with a rising JVP. What is the most likely complication?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Cardiac perforation with tamponade
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Manipulation of devices in the right heart can perforate a chamber or valve, causing pericardial tamponade. The triad of hypotension, tachycardia and a rising JVP during cardiac manipulation points to tamponade, requiring urgent echocardiography and surgical escalation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which access site is most commonly chosen for endovascular retrieval of a foreign body that has embolised to the SVC or right atrium?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Right common femoral vein
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The right common femoral vein is large-calibre and offers a straight venous route to the SVC and right heart, making it the standard access for snare retrieval. A generously sized sheath is placed so the captured fragment can be withdrawn intact.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 68-year-old with a solid renal mass needs biopsy to type the tumour and guide oncological treatment. Which sampling technique is most appropriate?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Core biopsy for histology
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Core biopsy retrieves a tissue core that preserves architecture, allowing tumour typing, immunohistochemistry and molecular analysis. This makes it the preferred technique for characterising solid organ tumours over FNA, which yields only cells.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient undergoes CT-guided biopsy of a peripheral lung nodule and afterwards becomes breathless with pleuritic chest pain. What is the most likely complication?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Pneumothorax
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Pneumothorax is the characteristic complication of percutaneous lung biopsy, presenting with breathlessness and pleuritic pain. A post-procedure CXR is routine to detect it, and a significant pneumothorax may require aspiration or a chest drain.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which pre-procedure step most directly reduces the risk of bleeding before a percutaneous liver biopsy?
options: Keeping the patient nil by mouth
Checking and correcting clotting/platelets and pausing anticoagulants
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Checking and correcting clotting/platelets and pausing anticoagulants
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Bleeding is the main serious complication of percutaneous biopsy. Checking INR/clotting and platelets, correcting derangement, and withholding anticoagulants and antiplatelets directly lowers this risk before the procedure.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A patient with decompensated cirrhosis, platelets of 40, INR 1.9 and tense ascites needs a liver biopsy for staging. Why is the transjugular route preferred here?
options: Any bleeding drains into the hepatic vein rather than the peritoneum, reducing bleeding risk
It provides direct visualisation of focal liver lesions for targeting
It eliminates all risk of cardiac complications during the procedure
It delivers a larger, better-quality tissue core than the percutaneous route
It avoids the need to correct clotting or check platelets beforehand
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Any bleeding drains into the hepatic vein rather than the peritoneum, reducing bleeding risk
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Because the needle remains within the vascular system, bleeding from the track decompresses back into the hepatic vein instead of the peritoneal cavity. This makes the procedure safer in coagulopathy, thrombocytopenia and ascites, which is exactly this patient's situation.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which additional measurement can be performed during a transjugular liver biopsy?
options: Central venous oxygen saturation for sepsis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG)
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The transvenous catheter position allows free and wedged hepatic venous pressures to be recorded and the HVPG calculated. This quantifies portal hypertension, with a gradient of 10 mmHg or more indicating clinically significant disease.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which complication is particularly associated with the catheter path used in transjugular liver biopsy?
options: Cardiac arrhythmia as the catheter passes through the right atrium
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Cardiac arrhythmia as the catheter passes through the right atrium
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The catheter transits the superior vena cava and right atrium en route to the hepatic vein, which can trigger arrhythmias. Continuous ECG monitoring throughout the procedure is used to detect this promptly.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A tumour scheduled for thermal ablation sits directly against a large hepatic vein. Which phenomenon most threatens complete ablation at this site?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Heat-sink effect
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Blood flowing through the adjacent large vein carries heat away from the ablation zone, cooling tissue near the vessel and risking residual viable tumour. Microwave ablation is chosen in this situation because it resists the heat-sink effect better than RFA.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which ablation modality generates a visible ice-ball that allows real-time monitoring of the ablation margin on CT?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Cryoablation
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Cryoablation uses freeze–thaw cycles that form an ice-ball clearly visible on cross-sectional imaging, letting the operator track the ablation zone directly. This visibility and lower associated pain make it useful for renal tumours and bone metastases.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 74-year-old man with a 2.5 cm hepatocellular carcinoma is unfit for surgery. What is an essential pre-procedure check before percutaneous ablation?
options: Coagulation screen including INR and platelet count
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Coagulation screen including INR and platelet count
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Percutaneous needle placement into a vascular organ carries a bleeding risk, so INR and platelets must be checked and any coagulopathy corrected beforehand. Anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs are also managed per protocol to minimise haemorrhage.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A 74-year-old woman has a painful L1 osteoporotic compression fracture unresponsive to 6 weeks of analgesia. Which MRI finding best indicates the fracture is acute and likely to benefit from vertebroplasty?
options: Marrow oedema (high STIR signal) within the L1 vertebral body
Complete fatty marrow replacement at L1
Uniform low T1 and low T2 signal indicating chronic sclerosis
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Marrow oedema (high STIR signal) within the L1 vertebral body
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Marrow oedema on STIR/T2 signifies an acute, unhealed fracture that is the active pain generator. Augmentation of an oedematous level correlates with better pain relief, which is why MRI is used for selection.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: During vertebroplasty the operator sees cement beginning to track posteriorly toward the spinal canal under live fluoroscopy. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Inflate a balloon tamp to push the cement forward
Continue injecting until the vertebral body is fully filled
Inject radiographic contrast to improve visualisation
Increase injection pressure to complete the fill quickly
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Stop the cement injection immediately
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: Posterior tracking of cement signals impending canal leak, which can compress the cord or nerve roots. Injection under continuous fluoroscopy is stopped the moment such extravasation is seen to prevent neurological injury.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: What is the principal theoretical advantage of kyphoplasty over vertebroplasty?
options: It permanently prevents any adjacent-level fractures
Balloon inflation creates a cavity allowing cement injection at lower pressure, reducing leak risk and partially restoring height
It avoids the use of PMMA cement entirely
It requires no correction of coagulation before the procedure
It can be performed without any imaging guidance
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Balloon inflation creates a cavity allowing cement injection at lower pressure, reducing leak risk and partially restoring height
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: The bone tamp forms a low-pressure cavity so cement can be delivered more controllably, theoretically reducing extravasation. The balloon also partially restores vertebral height and reduces kyphosis.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: A TIPS procedure creates a channel connecting which two structures?
options: Portal vein and inferior vena cava directly
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Portal vein and hepatic vein
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: TIPS establishes a low-resistance tract through the liver parenchyma linking a portal vein branch to a hepatic vein. This shunts high-pressure portal blood into the systemic venous circulation to decompress portal hypertension.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which complication is the characteristic major downside of TIPS?
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: New or worsening hepatic encephalopathy
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: By diverting portal blood past the hepatocytes, TIPS reduces hepatic detoxification and raises ammonia levels. This precipitates or worsens hepatic encephalopathy, the defining trade-off of the procedure.

investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.question: Which finding would most strongly contraindicate a TIPS procedure?
options: A patent portal vein on Doppler
Right heart failure with pulmonary hypertension
A prior successful variceal band ligation
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.answer: Right heart failure with pulmonary hypertension
investigations__NUCLEAR & INTERVENTIONAL.explanation: TIPS increases venous return and cardiac preload, so pre-existing right heart failure or pulmonary hypertension can be precipitated into decompensation. This is why echocardiography is performed before the procedure to screen the heart.
